abstract: |
    Climate change is projected to alter marine ecosystem structure and function 
    globally. Modelling these changes is challenging, partly because projections 
    of the future physical environment are uncertain, especially in highly 
    productive, and variable, ocean upwelling areas such as the Southern Benguela 
    Upwelling System (SBUS) off southern Africa. Here, the StrathE2E end-to-end ecosystem model is implemented for the SBUS. The model was forced 
    by a four-member ensemble of NEMO-ERSEM physical-biogeochemical model outputs. 
    The ensemble covers two different NEMO-ERSEM forcing models (CNRM-CM6-1-HR & 
    GFDL-ESM4) which provided driving data sets (2010 – 2069) for NEMO, each under
    two Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) and Relative Concentration Pathway (RCP)
    emissions scenarios (1-2.6: Sustainability – Taking the Green Road, and 3-7.0:
    Regional Rivalry – A Rocky Road).
    
    Net primary production and low trophic level guilds, such as zooplankton, 
    exhibit strongly diverging trajectories across the two NEMO-ERSEM forcing models. High 
    trophic level guilds such as birds, pinnipeds, and cetaceans are highly 
    sensitive to the parameterization of demersal fish, suggesting improvements 
    in our understanding of demersal fish in the region are important for 
    understanding and modelling the impacts of climate change on high trophic 
    level guilds. Environmental driver sensitivity analyses reveal that vertical mixing
    is highly important for variation in low trophic level guilds across these 
    forcing models. These findings highlight the sensitivity of the SBUS ecosystem
    to variation in wind-driven upwelling and downwelling, and especially the 
    need for advancements in monitoring and modelling of upwelling changes for 
    the region.

# Introduction

The Southern Benguela Upwelling System (SBUS) is a large Eastern Boundary Upwelling System
(EBUS) that extends around the western coast of South Africa, from the warm Agulhas current
in the south to the northern Benguela system (Namibia). The SBUS supports
highly productive recreational and large and small scale commercial fisheries
[@sumaila2016]. In particular, small-pelagic and Cape Hake fisheries
represent substantial food and employment provisioning for South Africa [@statuso2023; @kainge2020].

Primary and fisheries production in the Southern Benguela exhibit high seasonal and decadal
variability due to changes in environmental conditions such as temperature and upwelling
[@lamont2014]. Phytoplankton, the food-web base, experiences strong bottom-up
control, responding to upwelling and retention of nutrient-rich water
on the shallow shelf [@flynn2020; @martin2024; @cury2004]. Future conditions in EBUS under
climate change are highly uncertain due to a limited understanding of how, and by what
magnitude, wind-driven upwelling processes, and associated temperature and nutrient
conditions, may change [@bograd2023].

Southern Benguela ecosystem modelling under climate change has primarily focused on the independent
effects of temperature and primary production on the ecosystem [@lockerbie2019;
@ortega-cisneros2026; @eddy2025], with end-to-end modelling also incorporating upwelling
into forcing [@travers-trolet2014; @ortega-cisneros2018]. While modelling approaches differ
in their projections, multiple studies project declines in ecosystem biomass, and associated
fisheries yield, under increasing temperatures with differing direction and magnitude of
responses across functional groups [@ortega-cisneros2026; @eddy2025]. Additionally, previous
modelling studies show little agreement in ecosystem response to changes in upwelling
[@ortega-cisneros2018; @travers-trolet2014]. Previous explorations of ecological responses
using mechanistic models include few environmental variables and limited environmental
interactions, possibly reducing the scope of effects seen under explored simulations.

Understanding the influence of multiple climate drivers, and their interactions, on
ecologically and economically important guilds remains an important step towards mechanistic
projections of ecosystem functioning and services [@cooley2023].
End-to-end ecosystem models holistically represent physical, chemical and biological
processes driving climate change responses. However, increased model and forcing complexity
increases the difficulty of quantifying driver effects, leading to
simulations that incorporate limited drivers and their interactions. Variance-based Shapley
Effects originate from game theory [@shapley1953] and quantify the contribution
of input variable variance to output variance while accounting for non-linear interactions
between inputs [@song2016]. Combining these modelling and analysis approaches can identify
of key drivers of model outputs, while accounting for high levels of
environmental and ecological complexity.

This investigation aims to assess potential impacts of climate change on SBUS ecosystem state. 
Using StrathE2E, a computationally efficient
end-to-end ecosystem modelling framework; a full-factorial environmental forcing simulation
design; and Shapley Effects, this investigation aims to identify causal relationships
between environmental drivers, ecosystem state and uncertainty, while accounting
for holistic environmental interactions. Quantifying the relative importance of 
environmental drivers for various ecosystem guilds and their uncertainty will
help target regional modelling and monitoring efforts, enhancing future mechanistic
projections of the ecosystem under climate change [@cooley2023].

# Methods

## Project overview

This investigation uses the StrathE2E end-to-end ecosystem model (**Box 1**). To assess
potential impacts of climate change on the Southern Benguela Upwelling System, environmental forcing data were extracted from NEMO-ERSEM outputs across six
decades (2010-2069), two Shared-Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs 1-2.6 and 3-7.0) and two NEMO-ERSEM forcing
models [@artioli2023; @butenschön2016; @gurvan2019]. To identify key drivers of guild mass
under climate change full-factorial permutation sensitivity analyses are used
(@fig-method-outline; B), first across decades and second across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models. Variance-based Shapley Effect values quantify variable contributions to guild mass variance across permutations.

In all analyses, StrathE2E models were run for a 49 year spin-up period to ensure steady
state, extracting final year outputs. Simulations were performed using the R
programming language [@rcore2025] and StrathE2E2 package [@heath2021]. Subsequent analyses
were conducted using the Julia programming language and Makie visualization system [@bezanson2017; @danisch2021]. 
Investigation code can be found at [@grier2026].

## Box 1: StrathE2E Marine Ecosystem Model Description

StrathE2E combines a dynamic model of marine ecology and a static model of fishing activity,
coded as a package for the R computing environment (Heath et al. 2021). The ecology model is
a set of coupled ordinary differential equations representing the continuous-time rates of
change in nitrogen mass of 26 non-living and living guilds of material due to flows through
a food web network. The guilds span dissolved inorganic nutrient, detritus and microbes,
through classes of plankton, benthos and fish to birds and mammals. The flows represent
predation, food assimilation, metabolism, excretion, demographic transitions (for fish and
benthos guilds; spawning and recruitment), passive advection, active migrations, and fishery
harvest. The spatial resolution is coarse, in keeping with the guild granularity of the food
web - an “inshore” and “offshore” zone, linked by advection and migration. Each zone is
further subdivided into 4 seabed habitats and, in the offshore zone, 2 water column layers.
The seabed habitats are biogeochemical compartments with discrete rates of processing
detritus mineralization and nutrient recycling constrained by sediment grain size, and the
sensitivity of these to disturbance e.g. by fishing abrasion. External environmental drivers
are monthly resolution annual cycles of time-varying physical and chemical data
(temperatures, marine hydrodynamics and river hydrology, sea surface light, turbidity, and
boundary data on inorganic nutrient concentrations and volumetric fluxes of water). The
model outputs state variable nitrogen masses of each guild in each compartment and the flows
between them, at daily intervals.

The StrathE2E fishing model integrates externally defined properties of up to 12 fishing
*métiers* - groups of vessels defined by the fishing gears they use - which selectively
harvest distinctive sets of guilds in the ecology model. Properties of each *métier* are
their habitat-level spatial distributions of activity rate, selectivity for ecology model
guilds, discarding, offal generation and seabed abrasion rates. The outputs from the fishing
model are integrated zone and guild-level fishing mortality, discarding and offal generation
rates, and habitat-level seabed abrasion rates. These are injected as parameters into the
ecology model and assumed to remain constant over all upcoming years of simulation.

## Model domain and spatial compartments

This investigation models the SBUS, extending from the northern South
Africa Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) border along the west coast to the Agulhas Bank in the
south (@fig-habitat-map). The Agulhas Current is a warm-water Western Boundary current that flows southwards
along the eastern coast of Southern Africa. The Agulhas Current terminates at the western
edge of the Agulhas Bank, where the Benguela current begins transporting upwelled cold water
northwards along the western coast. This creates a distinct divide in environmental
conditions in currents to the east and west of the Agulhas Bank [@lutjeharms2006], while
injection of warm water into the start of the Benguela Current enhances mixing
[@veitch2017]. For more information on model domain designation, see Supplementary File 2: Model Domain.

## Environmental driving data

Environmental driving data inputs to StrathE2E are monthly resolution time series, averaged within decades. Data were extracted from the outputs, and inputs, of four variants of a global, quarter-degree resolution NEMO-ERSEM
biogeochemistry model [@butenschön2016; @gurvan2019; @artioli2023]. Additional driving
variables, such as suspended mineral particulate matter and inshore wave height,
had no basis for future projections and are assumed to have a constant annual cycle
in future decades. For information on all environmental variables and sources see Supplementary File 2: Ecological drivers.

The four variants were defined by two atmospherically forced climate models
(CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4) [@voldoire2019; @dunne2020], and two
Shared-Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs 1-2.6 and 3-7.0) [@oneill2014], which provided inputs to
NEMO-ERSEM model runs. SSP1-2.6 was selected as a climate mitigation scenario, while
SSP3-7.0 represented a contrasting plausible future under increasing future emissions
[@hausfather2020]. CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4 were chosen for contrasting climate
sensitivity levels. GFDL-ESM4 has an equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) value of
2.7-3.4°C [@dunne2020], while CNRM-CM6-1-HR has a higher ECS of 4.34°C [@jones2023], meaning
CNRM-CM6-1-HR represents a greater level of atmospheric warming for the same amount of CO2
increase compared to GFDL-ESM4.

## Parameterization for Southern Benguela

To implement StrathE2E (**Box 1**) for the SBUS, region-specific
inputs from literature and regional expert
knowledge were collated for the 2010-2019 period where possible (@stbl-model-inputs). This includes
input data representing fishing fleets and their catch of
modelled guilds, biological event timing data for key regional species for each guild and
observational target data for parameter optimization of the ecosystem model. Fitted parameter 
calibration involved using simulated annealing to seek parameter values providing maximum likelihood of a suite of empirical 'target' data
on ecosystem and fisheries states during the baseline (2010-2019)
calibration period [@heath2021] (@stbl-model-inputs). StrathE2E
models were calibrated individually for CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4 to preserve differing
representations of baseline conditions, resulting in a "CNRM-CM6-1-HR StrathE2E
model" and a "GFDL-ESM4 StrathE2E model". For more information on data sources, parameterization and 
calibration see Supplementary File 2.

## Projected climate change impacts

Under four possible future scenarios and six decades modelled steady state nitrogen mass
values were averaged across the domain area for each guild. Monte Carlo
simulations were performed using ecological parameter values randomly sampled from uniform distributions,
weighting model outputs according to observational target data likelihood (see Supplementary
File 2 for information on target data) to calculate 95% credible intervals [@heath2021].
Sampled parameters include all fitted parameters such as diet preferences and nitrogen
uptake rates, as well as fixed parameters such as guild Q~10~ values and background
metabolic rates. All parameters were sampled using a coefficient of variation of 0.15. For each model parameterization, 
1000 parameter combinations were sampled and applied to variants (total 24,000 model runs). Final year steady state outputs are visualized as decadal time series.

To explore ecosystem state variance under climate change principal component
analysis (PCA) was conducted on best-fit steady state mass values, rotating multivariate guild mass
values along two principal components. The average vector between decade Principal Component (PC) values and average vector between
forcing models in PC space were calculated to identify guilds contributing strongly to signals of ecosystem PCA variance. Each guild's contribution was quantified as the angle
between guild mass PCA loading and the two variation vectors, selecting guilds that
correlate with across decade and forcing model variation for further analyses.

## Identifying important climate change drivers

To quantify the influence of environmental driving data on ecosystem state under
different contexts (climate forcing models, SSPs, decades), variable group contributions to ecosystem outcomes were calculated using full-factorial permutations. Permutation analyses were informed by biomass PCA results and performed for
key signals of projection uncertainty. Firstly, across decades to identify drivers of guilds with
strong trends across time and secondly, across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models to identify drivers of
guilds that diverge between GFDL-ESM4 and CNRM-CM6-1-HR projections. Guilds with a PCA loading angle of less than 30° to vectors of across
decade variance and across NEMO-ERSEM forcing model variance respectively were selected for analyses. Additionally, Net Primary Production was included in output analyses to investigate drivers of change in system
productivity. Driving variables were grouped according to
@tbl-variable-groups, and then permuted in full-factorial combinations
(@fig-method-outline). Annual mass results were collated for each target guild to calculate
the variance-based Shapley Effect value of each variable for each guild [@song2016].

#### Shapley effects

Shapley Values quantify the contribution of a variable to an output value [@shapley1953]. Variance-based
Shapley Effects are an extension of Shapley Values, which are a fair way to calculate the
contribution of each variable to variance in a given output [@song2016]. By calculating
the contribution of an input to all possible coalitions of other variables, Shapley Effects incorporate interactions
between variables, using a full factorial permutation set to calculate exact values. Shapley Effects
offer an advancement over common sensitivity metrics such as first-order effects by effectively
incorporating input interactions [@song2016].
Variance-based Shapley Effects quantify variable group contributions to guild output variance.
For further explanation of Shapley Effect calculations and permutation runs see Supplementary File 1.

#### Identifying key drivers across decades

Variable permutations were performed across three decades (2010-2019, 2030-2039 and 2060-2069)
within the four climate scenarios. Seven variable groups vary across
decades, with three possible sets of values per climate scenario (forcing model - SSP
combination) (@tbl-variable-groups). Results are presented for guilds that are strongly
associated with ecosystem variance across decades (@sfig-pca-separation), and net
primary production.

Model permutations were additionally used to
identify model runs where combinations of variable groups are changed to 2060-2069, while
other variables remain at a 2010-2019 baseline. These model runs are used to assess the
influence of variable group interactions and prevalence of non-linear interactions
between variable groups.

#### Identifying key drivers across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models

Permutations of variables were performed across forcing models, within each of the six decades and
SSPs analysed. Permutations are completed once for each
model parameterization (CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4 StrathE2E parameterization). Six variable groups vary across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models, with two
sets of values per decade and SSP (@tbl-variable-groups). Results are presented for guilds strongly associated with ecosystem variance across
NEMO-ERSEM forcing models (@sfig-pca-separation),
and net primary production.

# Results

## Future climate impacts

Both CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4 StrathE2E models
experienced high levels of parameter uncertainty for mass value predictions
(@sfig-biomass-timeseries; @sfig-biomass-pca-mc). Despite low confidence in absolute mass projections,
guilds experience higher confidence for modelled directions and magnitudes of change
under increasing climate pressures (@fig-percent-biomass-timeseries). This suggests that
mechanisms driving climate-related changes, particularly for plankton and benthos guilds,
are not sensitive to parameter changes. Ecosystem net primary productivity is projected to
substantially increase across decades under GFDL-ESM4 NEMO-ERSEM forcing model
(@fig-percent-biomass-timeseries) and decrease under CNRM-CM6-1-HR forcing model.

Demersal fish, demersal fish larvae, pinnipeds and cetaceans are particularly sensitive to
changes in model parameters (@fig-percent-biomass-timeseries), experiencing broader credible
intervals than lower trophic level guilds. Guild production rates for demersal fish show
that modelled demersal fish gain greater nitrogen mass from recruitment than from
consumption, with recruitment sustaining net production at a positive level
(@stbl-dfish-biology). To investigate the influence of demersal fish larvae parameterization
on predatory guilds a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis was performed on physiological parameters. Demersal fish larvae
density dependent mortality; nitrogen uptake half-saturation coefficient; and maximum
nitrogen uptake rate parameters control biomass growth and recruitment into adult demersal
fish. These parameters were sampled in 100 evenly spaced steps from -25% to +25% of the base
parameter value from CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4 models respectively, resulting in 300 runs
for each of the two models. Local sensitivity analyses revealed that planktivorous fish,
demersal fish, pinnipeds, birds and cetaceans are highly sensitive to demersal fish larvae
maximum nitrate uptake rate and nitrogen uptake half-saturation coefficient values
(@sfig-dfishlar-sensitivity).

Principal Component Analysis highlights the influence of decadal changes and NEMO-ERSEM
forcing model choice on overall modelled ecosystem masses. The first two principal
components explain 72% of ecosystem mass variance. Benthos Suspension/Deposit Feeders,
Omnivorous zooplankton, surface layer Phytoplankton, total nitrogen mass and Carnivorous
zooplankton align strongly with ecosystem state changes across the forcing models
(@fig-biomass-pca, B; @sfig-pca-separation). Pinnipeds, Demersal fish, deep layer
Phytoplankton, Birds, Benthos Carnivorous/Scavenge Feeders and Cetaceans align strongly with
ecosystem changes across decades (@fig-biomass-pca, B; @sfig-pca-separation). There is
little variation in ecosystem state across SSPs.

## Drivers of temporal ecosystem change

For guilds strongly correlated with temporal ecosystem change, Shapley Effect environmental
variable contribution values indicate that only temperature, boundary flow and vertical
mixing driving variables contribute to variance in modelled mass levels (@fig-across-decade-shap). When forced by
CNRM-CM6-1-HR, under SSP3-7.0 the contribution of temperature to mass variance increases
from SSP1-2.6. Under CNRM-CM6-1-HR, temperature is a stronger driver of variation for
pinnipeds, birds and cetaceans compared to deep layer phytoplankton, carnivorous/scavenge
feeding benthos and demersal fish guilds. When forced by GFDL-ESM4, three of the six guilds
are primarily driven by boundary flows and three are primarily driven by vertical mixing,
with all guilds having low importance of temperature. Deep layer phytoplankton has distinct
Shapley Effect values to other assessed guilds, with \>75% of variance attributed to
vertical mixing under all forcings. Interactions between environmental variable groups
influence guild mass outcomes in an additive manner (variable 1 effect + variable 2 effect),
suggesting variable interactions are not influential in the model
(@sfig-var-interaction-hist).

GFDL-ESM4 forcing data show a greater degree of seasonal variability in vertical diffusivity
and offshore upwelling and downwelling compared to CNRM-CM6-1-HR
(@sfig-driver-vertical-mixing). In StrathE2E, temperature influences the metabolism and prey
uptake rates for consumer guilds, while boundary flows and vertical mixing influence
distributions of nitrogen and plankton guilds across domain boxes, affecting predator
distributions and nutrient uptake.

## Drivers of variance across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models

For guilds correlated with ecosystem state separation across the NEMO-ERSEM forcing models,
Shapley Effect contribution values indicate high contribution from vertical mixing
(@fig-across-esm-shap). Boundary flows have the second highest contribution to
across-forcing model mass variance for almost all guilds assessed. Variable groups such as
nutrient concentrations, river outputs, light and temperature have low contributions.
Variable group contributions are similar across the best-fit CNRM-CM6-1-HR and GFDL-ESM4
parameterizations, highlighting consistent mechanisms of change (@fig-across-esm-shap).

The choice of NEMO-ERSEM CMIP6 model forcing StrathE2E strongly influences projected
ecosystem outcomes (@fig-biomass-pca). The two forcing models project different future wind
fields in the region, resulting in distinct NEMO-ERSEM projections of upwelling and
downwelling (@sfig-driver-vertical-mixing; @sfig-ssp3-winds-cmip). Under these projections,
low trophic level guilds and net primary production display diverging best-fit model
trajectories. Vertical mixing contributes the most (\>60%) to variance for the majority of
these guilds.

# Discussion

StrathE2E modelling for the Southern Benguela ecosystem is consistent with observational and modelling literature that suggests a strong influence of
climate variability and change on the system [@fig-biomass-pca; @shannon2009; @blamey2015]. There have been contrasting suggestions about spatially complex long-term
upwelling and warming trends experienced in the Southern Benguela system [@blamey2015;
@vanderlingen2018]. Additionally, range shifts in multiple species have been documented,
likely driven by periods of intensified upwelling [@vanderlingen2018]. While offshore
temperatures have increased, periods of coastal cooling have led to changes in planktivorous
fish distributions around Cape Agulhas [@roy2007; @vanderlingen2018]. Fine scale
oceanographic monitoring along with biogeochemical modelling and validation of climate model
behaviour with observed trends may help to reduce uncertainty in climate and ecosystem model
projections for the region.

This investigation identified temperature, vertical mixing and boundary flows as key
variable groups influencing change in high trophic level guilds across decades.
@ortega-cisneros2018 modelled the effects of climate change on the ecosystem using an
Atlantis end-to-end model forced by low (RCP 2.6) and high (RCP 8.5) emission futures.
Atlantis modelling projected declines for most functional groups including top predators
such as Cetaceans, seabirds and demersal fish including sharks, with temperature being
suggested as a strong driver [@ortega-cisneros2018]. This is supported by our CNRM-CM6-1-HR
results, which found high importance of temperature. On the other hand, modelling with
Atlantis [@ortega-cisneros2018] and ROMS-N~2~P~2~Z~2~D~2~-OSMOSE [@travers-trolet2014] found
that changes in vertical mixing (under RCP 8.5) did not influence high trophic level guilds.
Distinct magnitudes, directions and mechanisms of change suggest a high influence of
structural (ecosystem model) uncertainty for the Southern Benguela system.

Structural uncertainty arises due to choices made in the construction and implementation of
ecosystem models such as the resolution of components (spatial, temporal, taxonomic) and
relationships/links represented [@payne2016]. @ortega-cisneros2026 quantified uncertainty
across a Southern Benguela ecosystem projection ensemble containing 2 marine ecosystem
models (Atlantis and EwE), and 2 Earth System Models (ESMs) and 2 SSPs used for temperature
and primary production forcing data. @ortega-cisneros2026 found ecosystem model structural
uncertainty accounted for more than 50% of projection
variance for groups such as demersal fish and zooplankton, with uncertainty
between ESMs also contributing substantially to variance across groups. @eddy2025 found strong divergence in overall biomass projections for the system across
regional ecosystem models. While results of this investigation find substantial contribution of NEMO-ERSEM forcing models
to uncertainty (@fig-biomass-pca), we also find strong contribution of parameter uncertainty, which was not previously considered [@ortega-cisneros2026; @eddy2025] (@fig-percent-biomass-timeseries; @sfig-biomass-pca-mc). Incorporating StrathE2E into a three model ensemble with Atlantis and EwE to quantify
paramter, structural and scenario uncertainty would
further enhance model development and decision support.

Idenitification of vertical mixing as the primary driver of low trophic level guild variance is supported by literature
suggesting that bottom-up control leads to high variability across spatial and temporal
scales due to upwelling [@cury2004; @martin2024; @lamont2014].
There is little consensus on how this ecosystem, and other EBUS globally, may
change in the future due to high levels of uncertainty around future upwelling
[@bograd2023; @garcía-reyes2015]. In a global comparison of EBUS NPP
projections (including the Southern Benguela) using 13 CMIP6 models @cioffi2025 found that
differences in upwelling-favourable winds resulted in substantial variation in
both direction and magnitude of NPP projections. These conclusions are supported by the
results of this investigation (@sfig-ssp3-winds-cmip; @sfig-driver-vertical-mixing;
@fig-percent-biomass-timeseries). A formal assessment/validation of NEMO-ERSEM's
representation of upwelling, along with validation of wind projections obtained from climate
models would improve confidence in subsequent ecosystem model applications in EBUS regions.

In the face of high uncertainty and diverging projections,
climate change impact investigations would benefit from comparisons of a broad range of
ecosystem models, model parameterizations, and environmental forcing scenarios [@eddy2025;
@maury2025]. Approaches such as Decision Making Under Deep Uncertainty involve exploring many possible ecosystem futures, helping to identify trajectories of environmental
conditions, ecosystem responses or management decisions that may lead to critical outcomes
[@kalra2014]. Exploring a broader range of futures (forcing models and SSPs) could help to
identify critical patterns of upwelling that may lead to poor ecosystem states, allowing the
focusing of monitoring and trend assessment efforts.

The results of this investigation highlight ecosystem components and drivers that should be
prioritized for further investigation. Greater parameter uncertainty than future scenario
uncertainty, for high trophic level guilds in particular, suggests data collection and model
selection are important areas of focus. Additionally, improved understanding and projection
of wind-driven upwelling trends under climate change will be important for projecting
ecosystem state into the future, particularly for low trophic level guilds. Approaches such
as near-term ecological forecasting may offer a pathway to iteratively incorporate such
advancements in ecological and climate change understanding in the region at timescales
relevant to management decisions [@dietze2024].

## Limitations

High parameter uncertainty in the presented models may be due to biased or inconsistent
target data used for fitting [@hilborn1992]. Additionally, identifying best-fit parameter
values increases in difficulty as model complexity increases [@preston2025].
@ortega-cisneros2018 provided error estimates across subsets of Atlantis parameters
controlling plankton guilds' growth rates, however computational limitations prevented a
quantification of global parameter uncertainty. This investigation represents the first
end-to-end marine application of best practice recommendations for quantifying parameter
uncertainty [@simmonds2024]. While parameter uncertainty decreases forecast
precision, this may not prevent effective decision support but requires the use of
alternative decision support methods such as management outcome distribution evaluation
[@ascough2008; @reichert2005].

While parameterized using data spanning 2010-2019 where possible, target data for guild
production rates and P:B ratios were sourced from ecological models of the 1970-2015 period
that used departmental survey data to model fisheries [@shannon2020]. As official fisheries
data were not made available, this investigation used reconstructed fisheries data for the
2010-2019 period from Sea Around Us [@zeller2017] with domestic fleet uncertainty scores
ranging from "low" ($\frac{+}{-}$ 30%) to "very low" ($\frac{+}{-}$ 50%)
(@sfig-sau-uncertainty). Reconstructed catch timeseries for Sardines, Anchovies, Herring and
Cape Hakes closely match those reported in @statuso2023. Improved completeness and quality
of parameterization and calibration data may help to reduce parameter uncertainty and
improve the representation of guilds in the model. For more information on the
parameterization process see Supplementary File 2.

Interpretation of demersal fish and top-predator guilds using these StrathE2E
implementations must consider that demersal fish biological event timing parameters reflect
available literature for Cape Hake species (*Merluccius capensis* and *Merluccius
paradoxus*) only (Supplementary File 2). It has been suggested that Cape Hake in the
northern Benguela region (Namibia) experience high annual variability in stock biomass
[@macpherson1991] driven by variable recruitment [@kainge2013]. This likely reflects the
sensitive parameterization of demersal fish in the Southern Benguela models presented.

## Future work

While improved calibration data can increase model forecast precision, validation with
independent data, particularly for responses to climate change, can improve decision support
confidence [@lubianabotelho2025]. @ortega-cisneros2017 performed hindcast skill assessment
of a regional Atlantis model, identifying variable performance across modelled species,
however data independent of model calibration was not available. Subject to data
availability, validation of the best-fit southern Benguela StrathE2E models presented in
this investigation using independent observational data would improve confidence in the
presented conclusions and ecosystem projections.

Observational studies have suggested that trends in fishing in the region may interact with
climate change driven environmental trends in the region, altering the hazards experienced
by species [@jarre2015; @ramírez2022]. Using StrathE2E to explore the interacting effects of
many climate and fishing scenarios may improve knowledge available for management decisions.
Using a protocol such as Ocean System Pathways (developed by FishMIP - the Fisheries and
Marine Ecosystems Model Intercomparison Project), which outlines a standardized approach for
modelling the influence of future climate change and fisheries trends on marine ecosystems
would allow StrathE2E to contribute to valuable model intercomparison investigations for
this highly variable region [@maury2025].

## Conclusion

This investigation uses StrathE2E models to explore possible consequences of future climate
change on the Southern Benguela Upwelling ecosystem. Climate change sensitivity analyses
reveal a strong influence of vertical mixing, particularly for low trophic level guilds.
Future scenario uncertainty (due to uncertain projections of upwelling related winds)
strongly influences future ecosystem projections, identifying a key area for improved
monitoring and modelling. While this investigation reveals that temperature, vertical mixing
and boundary flows may be important for high trophic level guilds, high parameter
uncertainty and sensitivity are present. Sensitivity to demersal fish parameterization
highlights where improvements in the representation and parameterization of guilds, as well
as observational calibration data, would improve understanding and projection of climate
change impacts. Inter-comparisons of regional ecosystem models under climate change,
focusing on mechanisms of climate impacts will be valuable to reduce uncertainty and
understanding of future change.

## Shapley Effects

The following equations were used to calculate variance-based Shapley Effects 
[@eq-shapleyvalue; @shapley1953; @song2016], quantifying the contribution of variable groups to variance in guild outputs.
$$
\phi_j(val) = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{j\}} 
   \frac{|S|!(p-|S|-1)!}{p!}\,\big(val(S \cup \{j\}) - val(S)\big)
$$ {#eq-shapleyvalue}

Where $\phi_j$ is the Shapley value for variable $j$, $S$ is a subset of input variables not
including $j$, $p$ is the number of possible coalitions of variables that do not include
$j$. To extend this calculation to variance-based Shapley Effects [@song2016] on discrete
inputs (levels = model variants), $val(S)$ is substituted for [@eq-varexplained; @song2016],
calculating the output variance explained by inputs from a set of variables $S$. The
resulting Shapley Effect ($\phi_j$) represents the sum of marginal contributions of variable
$j$ to all coalitions of other input variables. By calculating the contribution of $j$ to
all possible coalitions of other variables, Shapley Effects incorporate the interactions
between variables, using a full factorial permutation set to calculate exact Shapley
Effects.

$$
Var[E[Y|X_S]]
$$ {#eq-varexplained}

@eq-varexplained is used to calculate the variance in conditional means of output $Y$ across
levels of inputs from input set $X_S$.

To calculate variable group Shapley Effect values for guilds, model outputs must
be collated from model permutations. Model permutations (runs) must include all
possible coalitions of variable group data sources (@fig-method-outline; @tbl-variable-groups).
To calculate the number of model permutations required for full-factorial simulations,
@eq-permutation-number can be used.

$$
N = d ^ v * r
$$ {#eq-permutation-number}

Where $d$ is the number of data sources available for permutation, $v$ is the number
of variable groups being permuted across data sources, and $r$ is the number of
independent replication levels. For across-decade permutations, there are 3 decades
in the dataset ($d$), 7 variable groups being permuted ($v$) and 4 climate scenario
replications ($r$) (NEMO-ERSEM forcing models and SSPs), resulting in a total of 8,748 model runs.
For permutations across NEMO-ERSEM forcing models, there are 2 forcing models in the dataset ($d$),
6 variable groups being permuted across them ($v$), and 24 replication levels formed by
6 decades, 2 SSPs and 2 model parameterizations, resulting in a total 1,536 model runs.

## Supplementary results

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: asis

cap = """
Biological values and rates for demersal fish and demersal fish larvae guilds when modelled for 2010-2019 (and 2060-2069 for larvae) using GFDL-ESM4 and CNRM-CM6-1-HR StrathE2E models under SSP3-7.0. Values represent the outputs from the final model year after running to steady state. `T_uptake` represents the total uptake of nitrogen by the guild. `T_defec_excr` represents the total nitrogen output by the guild as a result of metabolism and excretion. `Recruitment` represents the total nitrogen gained through recruitment of larvae to adults. `Spawning` represents the total nitrogen gained through spawning. `Net_Prod_feeding` represents conversion rate of nitrogen ingested to mass, less nitrogen lost through excretion (T_uptake - T_defec_excr). `Net_Prod` represents the total rate of nitrogen gained including recruitment and spawning processes (Recruitment + Spawning + Net_Prod_feeding). Recruitment reliance can be seen where `Recruitment` contributes greater mass to the guild than `T_uptake`.
"""
using Markdown, Tables, MarkdownTables, CSV, DataFrames, Format
cd("../src")
dfish_rates = CSV.read("./../outputs/initial_runs/demersal_fish_rates_variants_filtered.csv", DataFrame)
for col in names(dfish_rates)[names(dfish_rates) .!= "Rate"]
    dfish_rates[!, col] = Format.format.(dfish_rates[:, col]; precision=3, positivespace=true)
end
print(
    """
    ::: {.table #stbl-dfish-biology}
    $(markdown_table(dfish_rates, String))

    $(cap)
    :::
    """
)
```
